explanations.explanation: Hilkiah the priest finds the Book of the Law of the LORD while the money is being brought out. Somebody went in to carry money out and came out holding Scripture. That's the best surprise anybody has ever found during repair work, friend. Everything after this hangs on that book.

This verse never mentions the ark. What Hilkiah the priest finds is the Book of the Law of the LORD. I get why the ark came to mind when someone finds a treasure in the temple. Hold on to the book, baker, because the rest of the story is about it.

No staff shows up in this verse. Hilkiah the priest finds the Book of the Law of the LORD. Aaron's staff is a fun guess, though, and I'd have been looking for it too. Stay with the book, friend, because it's about to change the whole kingdom.

The text says the book was given by Moses. Moses was Israel's leader, and this is the Book of the Law of the LORD that came through him. So this isn't some random scroll that rolled out from behind a shelf. It's the real Law, and it was found in the house of the LORD.

Aaron was Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), so I see how he got on the list. But the verse says the book was given by Moses. Aaron stood close to the story, and he just isn't the name on this one. Moses is the one, baker.

Joshua was Moses' assistant (Joshua 1:1), so he's in the right neighborhood. Still, the verse says the book was given by Moses. Moses is the name on this one, and Joshua is one more name to keep straight. Next time you see this one, think Moses.

explanations.answer: The money was paid to the supervisors and workers
explanations.explanation: That's right. Shaphan the scribe tells the king the money found in the house of the LORD has been paid out and put into the hands of the supervisors and workers. He says the servants are doing all that has been placed in their hands (2 Chronicles 34:16). Good report, baker, and then he gets to the book.

explanations.answer: The repairs on the house are all finished now
explanations.explanation: The report doesn't say the repairs are finished. Shaphan says the money has been paid out and put into the hands of the supervisors and workers. Notice that the work is still in their hands. Finished is a big claim, friend, and the text doesn't make it.

explanations.answer: The money for the repairs has all run out
explanations.explanation: Shaphan never says the money has run out. He says it has been paid out and put into the hands of the supervisors and workers. Paid out and run out sound close, but they mean different things. A scribe keeps careful records, baker, so I'd stick to his exact words.

That's true. After he tells the king that Hilkiah has given him a book, Shaphan reads it in the presence of the king. So Josiah doesn't just hear about the book. He hears it read right there in front of him.

The text says it plainly: Shaphan read it in the presence of the king. Josiah hears the words themselves, not a summary. That matters, because what he does next comes straight from hearing them. So this one is true, friend.

When the king heard the words of the Law, he tore his clothes. Later the LORD says Josiah's heart was tender, and that he humbled himself, tore his clothes and wept before Him (2 Chronicles 34:27). I think those words hit him hard, baker.

The verse says the king tore his clothes, not washed them. Nobody here is running a laundry, friend. When Josiah heard the words of the Law, he tore them. Later the LORD says Josiah humbled himself and tore his clothes.

He doesn't change his clothes. He tears them. That's a very different thing, baker, and I wouldn't try it on a good apron. The text says that when the king heard the words of the Law, he tore his clothes.

explanations.answer: Inquire of the LORD about the book
explanations.explanation: Josiah tells them, “Go and inquire of the LORD for me…” That's concerning the words in the book that has been found. He sends the men to ask the LORD about it, which tells you how seriously the king takes what he just heard.

explanations.answer: Make copies of the book for every city
explanations.explanation: Josiah never orders copies in this passage. His order is to go and inquire of the LORD concerning the words in the book that has been found. Copies for every city would be a big project, baker, and the text doesn't mention one. The order is to inquire of the LORD.

explanations.answer: Hide the book where it will be safe
explanations.explanation: No hiding happens here. Josiah has just heard the book read, and he sends five men to inquire of the LORD about it. Later he reads it aloud to all the people (2 Chronicles 34:30). That book is about as far from hidden as a book can get, friend.
Look at his words again. Josiah says to inquire of the LORD “…for me and for those remaining in Israel and Judah…” So the request covers more than himself. He's thinking about the people too, baker.

That's right. Josiah says, “Go and inquire of the LORD for me and for those remaining in Israel and Judah…” He includes himself, and he also includes the people still in Israel and Judah. The king isn't asking only for his own sake.

explanations.answer: Their fathers did not keep the LORD's word
explanations.explanation: Josiah says it's “…because our fathers have not kept the word of the LORD by doing all that is written in this book.” He's looking at what the book says and comparing it with what was done. He doesn't blame the paint or the roof. He names the word of the LORD that wasn't kept.

explanations.answer: The temple was left in ruins for years
explanations.explanation: Josiah doesn't give the state of the building as his reason. He says the wrath is great because their fathers have not kept the word of the LORD by doing all that is written in this book. The repairs are going on in this passage, but they aren't what he points to. The reason is the word that wasn't kept, friend.

explanations.answer: The people stopped giving to the temple
explanations.explanation: Giving isn't what Josiah mentions. He says it's because their fathers have not kept the word of the LORD by doing all that is written in this book. The money in this passage is going out to the workers, not missing. So the reason is the word that wasn't kept, baker.

That's right. Hilkiah and the king's men go and speak to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum. She lived in Jerusalem, and the LORD gives her the message for the king. She's the one they find with a word from Him.

Deborah was a prophetess who judged Israel (Judges 4:4), so I see why her name came up. But the men in this passage go to Huldah the prophetess. Deborah's story is in a different part of the Bible. Huldah is the one in Jerusalem, baker.

Anna was a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel (Luke 2:36), but she's in a different story. The men here go and speak to Huldah the prophetess. Huldah is the one living in Jerusalem, in the Second District. Don't let the prophetess title throw you, friend.

That's the word. The LORD says, “I am about to bring calamity on this place and on its people…” It's a hard message, and Huldah doesn't soften it. The king asked to hear from the LORD, and this is what comes back.

The LORD doesn't say rescue here. He says He is about to bring calamity on this place and on its people. It's a heavy word, and I wish it were an easier one. Later in the message there's a word just for Josiah, but this part is calamity.

Rest isn't the word in this message. The LORD says He is about to bring calamity on this place and on its people. I'd gladly hand you a nicer one, baker, but I won't change what the text says. This is a heavy part of the story.

That's true. The LORD says the calamity will come “…according to all the curses written in the book that has been read in the presence of the king of Judah…” So what He says lines up with what's written in the book. The book Josiah heard is the same one Huldah's message points to.

It's true, actually. The LORD says He will bring calamity “…according to all the curses written in the book that has been read in the presence of the king of Judah…” The message points right back to the book Shaphan read to Josiah. So the book and the message go together, baker.

explanations.answer: They forsook Him and burned incense to other gods
explanations.explanation: The LORD says it's “…because they have forsaken Me and burned incense to other gods…” The reason comes straight from Him, and He doesn't leave it vague. They turned away from Him and offered incense to other gods. That's the reason given, friend.

explanations.answer: They let His house fall apart for many years
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't give the state of His house as the reason. He says it's because they have forsaken Him and burned incense to other gods. The repairs are going on in this passage, but they aren't what He points to. Keep the reason where He puts it, baker.

explanations.answer: They turned to Egypt for help in their battles
explanations.explanation: Egypt isn't mentioned in this message. The LORD says it's because they have forsaken Him and burned incense to other gods. I'd skip adding reasons the text doesn't give, friend. Stay with His words.

The LORD says, “…because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before God when you heard His words…” A tender heart is one that can still be moved. Josiah heard the words and took them to heart. That's what the LORD notices about him.

Brave is a nice word, but it's not the one the LORD uses. He says Josiah's heart was tender and that he humbled himself when he heard His words. Sometimes the strongest thing a person does is let a hard word sink in. I think that's the point here, baker.

The LORD doesn't call Josiah's heart wise in this verse. He says it was tender, and that Josiah humbled himself when he heard His words. Tender is about being moved by what you hear. That's what He sees in the king.

The LORD says Josiah has humbled himself before Him, torn his clothes and “…wept before Me…” Then He says, “…I have heard you…” So the king's tears didn't go unnoticed. This is a sweet moment in a heavy chapter, friend.

It's true. The LORD says Josiah has torn his clothes and “…wept before Me…” and then adds, “…I have heard you…” The tears are right there in the message. I'd say that's a good moment to remember, baker.

explanations.answer: His eyes won't see all the calamity
explanations.explanation: The LORD says, “Your eyes will not see all the calamity that I will bring on this place and on its people.” He also says Josiah will be gathered to his grave in peace. This promise comes because Josiah humbled himself. The LORD heard him, and He answers.

explanations.answer: He will win every battle he fights
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't promise Josiah a winning record. His promise is that Josiah's eyes will not see all the calamity that He will bring. He also says Josiah will be gathered to his grave in peace. That's the promise on the page, friend.

explanations.answer: His name will be great among nations
explanations.explanation: A great name isn't part of this promise. The LORD says Josiah's eyes will not see all the calamity that He will bring on this place. He also says Josiah will be gathered to his grave in peace. That's what Josiah gets, baker, and it's what the text says.

explanations.answer: He reads them all the words of the book
explanations.explanation: That's what he does. In their hearing, Josiah reads all the words of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the house of the LORD. Everyone is there, great and small, priests and Levites too. The whole crowd gets to hear it, not just the king.

explanations.answer: He offers a great sacrifice to the LORD
explanations.explanation: No sacrifice is mentioned in this part of the story. Josiah goes up to the house of the LORD with the people, and he reads all the words of the Book of the Covenant in their hearing. The reading is the main event here. Keep your ears on the book, baker.

explanations.answer: He crowns his son as the next king
explanations.explanation: No crowning happens in this passage. Josiah goes up to the house of the LORD with all the people, great and small, and reads all the words of the Book of the Covenant in their hearing. Everybody called to one place? I'd have bet my last crumb on a coronation too, and I would've lost it. The only thing on the program is the reading, friend.

That's true. The text says Josiah read all the words of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the house of the LORD. It's the same book Hilkiah found, which earlier is called the Book of the Law. Same book, and it carries both names, baker.

It's true, friend. In their hearing, Josiah reads all the words of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the house of the LORD. Earlier it was called the Book of the Law. The text uses both names for the book that was found.

explanations.answer: To follow the LORD and keep His commandments
explanations.explanation: Josiah makes a covenant “…to follow the LORD and to keep His commandments, decrees, and statutes with all his heart and all his soul…” That's a full-hearted promise, not a half one. He also promises to carry out the words of the covenant written in the book. He heard the book, and now he's committing to it.

explanations.answer: To rebuild the walls around every city
explanations.explanation: Walls aren't part of this promise. Josiah makes a covenant to follow the LORD and keep His commandments, decrees and statutes with all his heart and all his soul. His promise is about following the LORD, not about building. It's a promise of the heart, baker.

explanations.answer: To send priests out to every nation
explanations.explanation: Josiah doesn't promise that here. He makes a covenant to follow the LORD and to keep His commandments, decrees and statutes with all his heart and all his soul. He also promises to carry out the words written in the book. That's the whole promise, friend.

explanations.answer: Take a stand in agreement to it
explanations.explanation: That's it. Josiah has everyone in Jerusalem and Benjamin take a stand in agreement to the covenant. So the promise isn't only the king's. The people stand with him, and then all the people of Jerusalem carry out the covenant of God.

explanations.answer: Bring a gift to the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: No gift is mentioned here. Josiah has everyone in Jerusalem and Benjamin take a stand in agreement to the covenant. The people are joining his promise, baker. That's what the text says.

explanations.answer: Fast and pray for three whole days
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention fasting or three days. Josiah has everyone in Jerusalem and Benjamin take a stand in agreement to the covenant. Keep it as simple as the text does, friend. They stand, and they agree.

The text says the opposite. “Throughout his reign they did not turn aside from following the LORD, the God of their fathers.” So for as long as Josiah was king, the people kept following. That's a good word to hear after all that heavy news, baker.

That's right. The text says, “Throughout his reign they did not turn aside from following the LORD, the God of their fathers.” So during Josiah's reign, the people kept following Him. After such a hard message, that's a bright line, friend.
